summary: Patterns and sequences teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of a repeating UNIT. The telling skills are abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest repeating unit — both of which, according to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013), cannot be done by visual matching alone and so reveal genuine structural understanding rather than surface copying. Build, extend, abstract, and isolate the unit, using units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation.
misconceptions: Extends a pattern by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping that there is a repeating unit.
Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer (makes ABAB for an ABB model).
Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit plus extra items that break the unit.

activities.title: Build, extend, and name the unit of repeat
steps: Continue a given model pattern, e.g. red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue — carry it on further with cubes, beads, or drawn shapes.
Circle or box the part that repeats and say where the pattern 'starts over'.

Name which items are the SAME and which is DIFFERENT: for red, blue, blue the two blues are the same and the red is the different cube that starts the chunk (spoken in order: different, same, same). The plain 'same, same, different' chant maps most cleanly to a two-same-then-different unit such as AAB.
activities.insight: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that repeats; the pattern is the unit, not just the next item you could add.

activities.title: Abstract the same KIND of pattern onto new materials
steps: Given a red-blue-blue model, use a different set (e.g. green and yellow cubes) to make 'the same KIND of pattern' — green, yellow, yellow, repeated.
Lay the new pattern directly under the model and check unit-for-unit: count how many yellows come before the next green.
Explain why your new pattern is the same kind even though the colours are different.
activities.insight: Making the 'same kind' of pattern means reproducing the STRUCTURE (one cube, then two matching cubes, then start over), not the colours — abstraction that colour matching alone cannot accomplish.

activities.title: Shrink to the smallest tower that keeps the pattern
steps: From a repeating pattern, build the smallest tower that still has the same pattern (for red-blue-blue, the three-cube unit red, blue, blue).
Decide whether removing cubes keeps or breaks the pattern, and explain why.
Try the same with AAB and ABC units, not just AB.
activities.insight: The smallest arrangement that preserves the pattern IS the unit of repeat; isolating it is the clearest sign of understanding structure.

activities.title: Describe the rule and connect to number sequences
steps: Say aloud the rule for a given sequence of objects ('it goes red, then two blues, then starts over').

Look at number sequences and skip-counting as patterns too, but notice the difference: in skip-counting (2, 4, 6, 8, …) the numbers keep growing and do not repeat, but the step does (add 2 each time). Some parts can repeat like a unit, e.g. the last digits when counting in 5s (5, 10, 15, 20 → 5, 0, 5, 0).
Create your own pattern with a chosen unit (ABB, AAB, or ABC) and challenge someone else to find the smallest unit.
activities.insight: Saying the rule out loud and making your own patterns help children move from 'what comes next' to thinking about the repeating unit. Number sequences such as skip-counting are a different kind of pattern: the numbers grow, and what repeats is the rule or step (e.g. +2), not a unit of items.

checkQuestion: Here is a pattern made with coloured cubes: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. First, carry it on for me. Now, using these different cubes (green and yellow), make the same KIND of pattern. Last, show me the smallest tower you could make that still keeps the same pattern.
checkAnswer: Extends the pattern preserving the red-blue-blue unit; abstracts the ABB structure into green-yellow-yellow (neither reverting to an AB alternation nor merely copying the colours); and offers the three-cube unit (green, yellow, yellow) as the smallest tower that keeps the pattern.
